title: Palindrome Partitioning
description: Brute force to optimized: rechecking every substring versus a precomputed palindrome table with instant lookups.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a string s, partition it into groups of substrings such that every substring in the partition is itself a palindrome. Return every possible such partitioning.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a string s, partition it into groups of substrings such that every substring in the partition is itself a palindrome. Return every possible such partitioning.

blocks.title: Analogy: Cutting a Ribbon Into Only Symmetric Pieces
blocks.text: Like cutting a printed ribbon into pieces where every single piece, once cut, must read the same forward and backward, and listing out every possible way to make such cuts.

blocks.caption: Every piece produced by the cuts must itself be a palindrome

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: s = "aab"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Partitioning","Every piece checked","Why"],"rows":[["[\"a\", \"a\", \"b\"]","each single character is trivially a palindrome","a single character always reads the same forward and backward"],["[\"aa\", \"b\"]","\"aa\" reads the same both ways, \"b\" is trivially a palindrome","both pieces satisfy the palindrome requirement"]]}

blocks.text: Example: s = "a"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Partitioning","Every piece checked","Why"],"rows":[["[\"a\"]","the only possible partitioning, trivially valid","a single character string has no other way to be cut"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: s with no repeated letters at all, like "abc"
Since no substring longer than 1 character can possibly be a palindrome here, the only valid partitioning is every character on its own, [["a", "b", "c"]].
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask exactly what work gets repeated across the many different branches of the recursive search, rather than assuming the enumeration itself is the bottleneck.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force backtracks through every possible way to cut the string, but re-verifies whether each candidate piece is a palindrome from scratch with a fresh character by character check, every single time that exact substring is considered.

Observation 2: The same substring boundaries recur constantly across many different branches of the search tree, so this identical palindrome check gets repeated over and over for no benefit.

Observation 3: Since the number of valid partitions can itself be exponential, backtracking is fundamentally unavoidable here, unlike Wildcard Matching or Interleaving String, which only ever needed a single yes or no answer; the real, meaningful optimization is removing the redundant palindrome rechecking, not the enumeration itself.

Observation 4: A substring is a palindrome exactly when its two endpoints match and the strictly smaller inner substring is also a palindrome, so this can be computed bottom up, from shorter substrings to longer ones, filling a full table once; confirmed by tracing s equal to "aab", where "aa" is correctly marked a palindrome from matching endpoints while "ab" and "aab" are correctly marked false, after which the exact same backtracking search now runs every check as an instant table lookup.

Recognizing that the exponential enumeration itself cannot be avoided, but the redundant palindrome rechecking absolutely can, is what turns a doubly expensive search into one backed by instant O(1) lookups.
6. Brute Force Solution
Recursively try every possible cut point from the current position, and at each candidate cut, check directly whether the substring up to that point is a palindrome before recursing on the remainder.
Step by step algorithm

items: Starting from the current position, try every possible end point for the next piece.
Check whether that candidate piece is a palindrome by directly comparing it to its reverse.
If it is, recurse on the remainder of the string, and if that recursion succeeds, record the completed partition.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every possible end point for the next piece is tried in turn, so no valid way of cutting the current position is missed.
The current path is built up and then popped after each recursive call returns, correctly restoring it before trying the next candidate end point.
Reaching the end of the string is exactly when the current path represents one complete, fully verified partition, worth recording.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possible cut sequence is explored, and only valid all palindrome partitions are recorded, so every correct answer is found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times 2 to the power n) in the worst case, since there can be exponentially many valid partitions, and checking each candidate substring for being a palindrome costs up to O(n).
Space: O(n), for the recursion stack and the current path being built.

Limitation: the exact same substring can get palindrome checked over and over again across many different branches of the recursion, since the same start and end positions recur constantly as different partitions are explored.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: every candidate substring is re-verified as a palindrome from scratch, even though the exact same substring boundaries are checked repeatedly across many different recursive branches.

What the exponential output means for this problem: unlike a yes or no question, enumerating every valid partition cannot be avoided, so the real target for optimization is the redundant per-check work, not the branching itself.

What a precomputed table fixes directly: a substring is a palindrome exactly when its endpoints match and its strictly smaller inner substring is also a palindrome, letting every substring's status be computed once, bottom up, from shorter to longer.

The core idea: build the full palindrome table once before backtracking begins, then let every check during the search become an instant O(1) lookup instead of a fresh character by character scan.

Precompute a table once, up front, where isPalin[i][j] records whether the substring from i to j is a palindrome, filled using the fact that s[i..j] is a palindrome exactly when s[i] equals s[j] and the inner substring s[i+1..j-1] is also a palindrome. With this table ready, the backtracking search can check any candidate substring in O(1) instead of re-scanning it character by character every time.
9. Optimized Solution
Precompute every substring's palindrome status once, then backtrack using instant lookups.
Dry run building the palindrome table for s = "aab"

blocks.content: {"headers":["Substring","Is palindrome"],"rows":[["\"a\" (index 0), \"a\" (index 1), \"b\" (index 2)","true, every single character is trivially one"],["\"aa\" (indices 0 to 1)","true, both characters match"],["\"ab\" (indices 1 to 2)","false, characters differ"],["\"aab\" (indices 0 to 2)","false, first and last characters differ"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: precompute every substring's palindrome status once, then backtrack with instant lookups

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because every substring's palindrome status depends only on strictly smaller, already computed substrings (its own endpoints and the inner substring one shorter on each side), so filling the table from the shortest substrings up to the full string guarantees every cell is correct by the time it is needed, and the backtracking search afterward never has to rescan a single character to check a candidate piece.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A substring's two endpoints match and its inner substring is already known to be a palindrome","The table marks this substring true","Longer palindromes are correctly built up from smaller verified ones"],["A substring's two endpoints do not match","The table marks this substring false immediately, with no need to check the inside at all","Non palindromic substrings are ruled out in constant time per entry"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) to precompute the table, plus O(n times 2 to the power n) for the backtracking itself, which is inherent to the number of valid partitions that may need to be output.
Space: O(n squared) for the table, plus O(n) for the recursion stack.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Palindrome Checks","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (recheck every candidate)","O(n times 2 to the power n)","O(n)","Recomputed from scratch on every single occurrence","Correct, but repeats identical checks constantly."],["Optimized (precomputed table)","O(n squared) plus O(n times 2 to the power n)","O(n squared) plus O(n)","Computed once, then looked up in O(1) every time","The expected answer, removing all redundant rechecking."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Since the number of valid partitions can itself be exponential, backtracking is fundamentally unavoidable to enumerate all of them, so the real, meaningful optimization here is removing the redundant palindrome recomputation, not trying to beat the exponential enumeration itself.
Common Mistakes

items: Rechecking whether a substring is a palindrome from scratch inside the backtracking loop instead of precomputing it once, which multiplies an already expensive search by an extra factor of the string length.
Forgetting to remove the most recently added piece from the current path before trying the next candidate end point, which corrupts every subsequent partition recorded.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A string of all the same character","Produces the maximum possible number of valid partitions, since every substring of it is a palindrome."],["A single character string","Has exactly one valid partitioning, itself."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Bring up the precomputed palindrome table proactively as soon as the brute force backtracking solution is working, since it is the expected natural follow up optimization for this exact problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid rechecking the same substring", think: precompute a full palindrome table once, then backtrack using instant lookups.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the exponential time entirely", think: no, since the number of valid partitions can itself be exponential, the output size alone forces that lower bound.
If the interviewer says "what if you only needed the minimum number of cuts", think: that becomes Palindrome Partitioning II, solvable with a pure DP over minimum cuts instead of enumerating every partition.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why can a substring's palindrome status always be computed from strictly smaller substrings?
Why is the exponential time complexity here considered unavoidable, unlike in Wildcard Matching or Interleaving String?
How would you adapt this approach to find only the minimum number of cuts needed, without enumerating every partition?
How would you count the total number of valid partitions without generating each one explicitly?
How would this approach change if pieces needed to be palindromes of at least a certain minimum length?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Longest Palindromic Substring, whose palindrome checking logic is the same underlying property, verified here for every possible substring instead of searched for the single longest one.
Wildcard Matching and Interleaving String, whose 2D tables also eliminate redundant recomputation, though those problems only needed a single yes or no answer rather than a full enumeration.

Any backtracking problem where the same candidate check recurs across many branches, where precomputing those checks once into a lookup table is a standard way to speed up the search without changing what it explores.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n times 2 to the power n) time, O(n) space. Optimized: O(n squared) time for precomputation plus O(n times 2 to the power n) for backtracking (inherent to the output size), O(n squared) space for the table.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: backtracking to enumerate every valid cut sequence, sped up by a precomputed palindrome table for instant substring checks.

Core Idea: a substring is a palindrome exactly when its endpoints match and its smaller inner substring is also one, so precomputing every substring's status once turns every check during backtracking into an instant lookup.
Time: O(n times 2 to the power n) for the brute force, O(n squared) plus the same O(n times 2 to the power n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(n squared) plus O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: when a problem's output size is itself exponential, the goal is not to beat that output size, but to eliminate wasted work performed while producing it.
Interview Difficulty: the backtracking structure is standard; recognizing that the precomputed table, not a smarter search, is the real optimization is the key insight.
One line memory trick: precompute every substring's palindrome status once, then let backtracking just look it up.
